This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Let $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ be the set of cubes. Is it true that\[1_A\ast 1_A(n) \ll (\log n)^{O(1)}?\]
#829: [Er83]
number theory
Mordell proved that\[\limsup_{n\to \infty} 1_A\ast 1_A(n)=\infty\]and Mahler [Ma35b] proved\[1_A\ast 1_A(n) \gg (\log n)^{1/4}\]for infinitely many $n$. Stewart [St08] improved this to\[1_A\ast 1_A(n) \gg (\log n)^{11/13}.\]
Additional thanks to: msellke

 Some easy to realize remarks. We are interested in the number of pairs $(x,y)$ of positive integers such that $x^3 + y^3 = n$. Set $s=x+y$, $t=|x-y|$, then $4n = s(s^2 + 3t^2)$, so for each divisor $s$ of $4n$ with $n < s^3 \leq 4n$ we determine $t$ uniquely and hence at most two possible pairs $(x,y)$, thus getting the upper bound $O(\tau(n))$ which is only $n^{o(1)}$. 
Each representation produces the integral point $X = \frac{12n}{s}$, $Y = \frac{36nt}{s}$ on the Mordell curve $Y^2 = X^3 - 432n^2$ with $X \mid 12n$. The requested estimate is thus a strong uniform bound for these special integral points. In particular, not only the shown constructions relate to specific elliptic curves, but the upper bound as well, as expected.
